::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Logical connectives in set-builder notation](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4666326/logical-connectives-in-set-builder-notation), asked by [Yenus](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1163821/yenus) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2023-03-25; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> I'm trying to understand what bi-implication and implication mean when they're used inside sets like in 
>
> 1. $$A = \{x\in \mathbb{N} \mid (x-1)(x-3)\neq 0 \iff  x+1=x\}$$
> 2. $$B = \{x\mid x\in \mathbb{N}  \land (x-1)(x-3)\neq 0 \iff  x+1=x\}$$
> 3. $$C = \{x\in \mathbb{N} \mid x \geq 3 \iff x <  0 \}$$
>
> What is the difference between sets $A$ and $B$ ? They both contain 
> natural numbers and I don't see how displaying an intersection makes a difference.
>
> If someone knows a source on the internet to better explain this or similar concepts, do share a link.
:::

For 1), $x + 1 = x$ is not satisfied by any natural number, so you can substitute FALSE. For $(x-1))(x-3) \neq 0 \iff \mathrm{FALSE}$ to be satisfied, you need to make sure $(x-1)(x-3) \neq 0$ is not satisfied. That is, it must be the case that $(x-1)(x-3) = 0$.  So $A = \{1,3\}$.

3) is quite similar. As for 2), I don't understand what $\cap$ means in this context. Neither “$x \in \mathbb{N}$” nor “$(x-1))(x-3) \neq 0 \iff x+1=x$” are sets.
